Sometimes it's not just about the price—it's about the perception.
A bag of chips? Open it and eat.
A candy bar? Peel the wrapper and enjoy.
Fresh fruits and vegetables? You might have to wash them, peel them, slice them, or cook them. That takes a little more time, so they feel like more work.
But when you compare prices, many fresh foods cost the same—or even less—than chips, candy, and soft drinks. Plus, they nourish your body, keep you fuller longer, and often feed more than one person.
An apple can cost less than a candy bar.
A few ears of fresh corn can cost less than a family-size bag of chips.
One watermelon can feed the whole family for about the price of two bags of chips.
Healthy eating isn't always about spending more money. Sometimes it's simply about making a different choice.
And when you buy fresh produce from your local farmers market, you're not only feeding your family—you’re supporting your neighbors and local farmers too.
What's your favorite fresh fruit or vegetable from the farmers market?

And Arkansas DHS has made a statement about this ruling that it doesn’t affect Arkansas.

That’s a quote from Oliver Anthony song “Rich Men North of Richmond,” and more facetious than anything.
Having said that, I have struggled with being overweight my entire life. I weighed 100 in 3rd grade and I completely understand the struggle you mention. I know how two people can eat the same thing and one be rail thin and the other person can get heavier.
Setting that aside, I think that a restriction on what type of foods a SNAP recipient can buy makes good sense. It is a “nutritional” program. The government. Takes from more fortunate people the fruit of their labor and distributes it to people who did not work for it. It should not be spent on a 12 pack of Mountain Dew and a bag of Doritos. It should be spent on actual food with a nutritional value.
just my two cents on the matter.
